text|A GUESTHOUSE IN THE HILLS ABOVE LUCCA
text|Six rooms in a stone farmhouse, a long table under the pergola, and forty hectares of olives that we pick by hand each November. Twenty minutes from Lucca, and a long way from anywhere.
text|A farmhouse that has fed itself from its own hill since 1780.

text|The house was built by a family of olive pressers, and the old press is still in the cellar, under the room that now carries its name. We moved here in 2014 with two children and no idea how to prune a tree.
text|Twelve years on, breakfast is our own bread, our neighbours’ eggs and figs from the wall by the pool; supper, four nights a week, is at one long table for everyone staying.
text|Up the tower’s own stair, with windows on all four sides.
text|The old olive press room, vaulted, and cool all summer.
text|The lemon house, opening onto the garden and the pool.
text|The hayloft, under the beams, with a bath by the window.
text|Off the loggia, looking west over the valley to the sea.
text|The old stables: two rooms, for a family.
text|Prices are a night for the room, with breakfast. Supper at the long table is €45 a head, wine from the hill included.
text|Wild asparagus in the hedges, the first swims, and the hills green for a few weeks.
text|Long days, the pool, and supper outside under the pergola until the swifts go to bed.
text|The harvest. Pick with us for a morning, and take home a litre of oil from your trees.
text|We close in January and February: the house rests, and so do we.
text|The harvest weeks are filling up.
text|From €180 a night, with breakfast. Free to cancel until thirty days before you come.

text|Perry pears once grew on four thousand acres here. Mary Holloway farms the last forty, and she isn’t sure who will farm them next.
text|By Tom Ashworth · A nine-minute read

text|THE TREES ARE OLDER THAN THE FARMHOUSE. Some of them went in when Victoria was a girl, and they’ve outlived every Holloway who planted them. A perry pear tree takes a lifetime to bear and then bears for two more: the saying in the Vale is that you plant pears for your heirs.

text|What Mary’s heirs will inherit is less clear. The cider makers who bought her fruit have gone over to apples, which crop in five years instead of fifty, and the last perry mill in the county closed in the spring. This autumn she pressed the harvest herself, in a borrowed press, in her own barn.
